author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars's apparent eastward drift, westward retrograde loop, and return to eastward motion during a typical retrograde episode.
Explain retrograde motion in the heliocentric model as a geometric consequence of Earth overtaking a slower outer planet.
Contrast geocentric epicycle-based explanations with the heliocentric explanation and explain why heliocentrism is more parsimonious.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for an outer planet based on relative orbital positions near opposition.
Compare Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn retrograde loops and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Mars in the Night Sky
modules.description: Students observe Mars tracing an apparent retrograde loop against labeled zodiac constellations over several months.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify Mars's usual eastward drift against the background stars.
Recognize the slowdown, westward reversal, and return to eastward motion during retrograde.
Describe retrograde as an apparent motion measured relative to fixed stars.
instructions: Look toward the virtual sky in front of you.
Step through the clips to follow Mars over several months.
Compare Mars only to the fixed background constellations, not to the horizon.

components.text: Leo   Virgo   Libra   Scorpio
Mars against the zodiac stars

clips.changeMeaning: The scene starts with Mars at the beginning of its normal prograde motion so students establish a baseline apparent direction against the fixed starfield.
clips.narration: From Earth, Mars usually drifts slowly eastward against the background stars. But every so often, something surprising happens.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is advanced eastward across the labeled constellations to show the usual slow prograde motion before any reversal begins.
clips.narration: Over the first part of this interval, Mars moves gradually eastward from one zodiac region to the next.

components.text: Station point: eastward motion slows

clips.changeMeaning: Mars reaches a station point where its eastward progress nearly stops, focusing attention on the impending reversal in direction.
clips.narration: Then Mars appears to slow down. Near the station point, its eastward progress nearly stops.

components.text: Retrograde: Mars moves westward

clips.changeMeaning: The trail is revealed and Mars is moved backward along it so students can see the westward part of the loop and its overall shape across the stars.
clips.narration: Now comes the puzzle. Mars reverses direction and moves westward for about two months, tracing the backward part of its loop across the sky.

components.text: Retrograde complete: eastward motion resumes

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is returned to a position beyond the loop, completing the observed pattern and framing retrograde as the phenomenon that later models must explain.
clips.narration: After another station point, Mars resumes its normal eastward drift. Explaining this backward loop was one of the central problems of pre-modern astronomy.

modules.description: Students examine how a geocentric model reproduces retrograde motion using a deferent and an epicycle centered on Earth.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify Earth, the deferent, and the epicycle in the geocentric model.
Explain how combined circular motions can generate an apparent backward loop.
Recognize that the geocentric explanation works but requires careful tuning.
instructions: Watch Mars move on the smaller epicycle while that circle moves on the larger deferent.
Notice when Mars is on the inner side of the epicycle nearest Earth.
Consider how many separate parameters must be adjusted to fit the observations.

components.text: Earth at center   |   Large circle: deferent   |   Small circle: epicycle

clips.changeMeaning: The geocentric mechanism is introduced with Mars riding on the epicycle so students can identify the two nested circular motions in the model.
clips.narration: In the geocentric model, Earth remains fixed at the center. Mars moves on a small circle called an epicycle, while the center of that epicycle moves on a larger circle called the deferent.

clips.changeMeaning: The epicycle center is moved along the deferent while Mars also shifts on the epicycle, illustrating how the two circular motions combine into a more complex path.
clips.narration: As both circles turn, Mars follows a combined motion. Most of the time, the net effect still carries it forward across the sky.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved to the inner side of the epicycle nearest Earth, where the combined motions produce the apparent backward motion of retrograde.
clips.narration: When Mars reaches the inner part of its epicycle, the small-circle motion can temporarily outweigh the large-circle motion. From Earth, Mars then appears to move backward.

components.text: Works, but needs tuned sizes, speeds, and added epicycles

clips.changeMeaning: The labels are updated to stress the explanatory cost of the epicycle model, connecting observational success with increasing complexity.
clips.narration: This model can reproduce the loop, but only by carefully choosing circle sizes and speeds. As observations improved, astronomers often had to add still more epicycles to preserve accuracy.

modules.description: Students view Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun and see retrograde arise naturally when faster Earth overtakes slower Mars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the relative orbital sizes and periods of Earth and Mars.
Explain why Earth overtakes Mars near opposition.
Recognize that heliocentric motion is smooth and does not contain physical loops.
instructions: View the solar system from above the orbital plane.
Track Earth's faster inner orbit and Mars's slower outer orbit.
Notice that the loop disappears in physical space.

components.text: Earth: 1 AU, 1 year   |   Mars: 1.52 AU, 1.88 years

clips.changeMeaning: Earth and Mars are placed on smooth orbit guides to establish the heliocentric geometry and their different orbital scales.
clips.narration: In the heliocentric model, the Sun sits at the center. Earth orbits at 1 astronomical unit in one year, while Mars orbits farther out at about 1.52 astronomical units in 1.88 years.

clips.changeMeaning: Both planets advance along their orbits, with Earth gaining on Mars to visualize the speed difference that leads to overtaking.
clips.narration: Because Earth is on the inner orbit, it moves faster. Over time, Earth catches up to Mars from the inside track.

clips.changeMeaning: The planets are positioned during the overtaking interval so students can identify the configuration associated with retrograde as seen from Earth.
clips.narration: Around opposition, Earth passes between the Sun and Mars. This is the key interval when Mars will appear to reverse direction in the night sky.

components.text: Two smooth orbits; no epicycles required

clips.changeMeaning: The planets are shown continuing on smooth paths after the pass, reinforcing that nothing loops physically in space even though a loop appears from Earth's viewpoint.
clips.narration: From outside the solar system, there is no physical loop in Mars's path at all. Retrograde emerges naturally from two smooth heliocentric motions, with no epicycles needed.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Linking Geometry to the Night Sky
modules.description: Students connect the heliocentric Earth-Mars line of sight to Mars's apparent sky position against the stars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate the Earth-Mars line of sight to Mars's apparent position in the sky.
Explain why that line of sight reverses direction during overtaking.
Recognize retrograde as a real geometric effect in apparent position.
instructions: Compare the orbital view on the left with the sky panel on the right.
Follow how Earth and Mars shift from clip to clip.
Notice how the apparent sky position reverses when the geometry reverses.

components.text: Line of sight maps orbital geometry to apparent sky position

clips.changeMeaning: The two synchronized views are aligned so students can match the Earth-Mars sightline with Mars's displayed position on the star panel.
clips.narration: Here the two perspectives are shown together. On the left is the heliocentric view; on the right is Mars's apparent position against the stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Before overtaking, the sightline and the sky position both shift eastward, showing how ordinary prograde motion appears in the night sky.
clips.narration: As Earth approaches Mars, the line of sight sweeps eastward through the constellations. In the sky view, Mars also drifts eastward.

components.text: During overtaking, the sightline reverses direction

clips.changeMeaning: At the overtaking geometry, the apparent sky position moves backward so students can explicitly connect retrograde to the reversal of the Earth-Mars viewing direction.
clips.narration: As Earth overtakes Mars, the line of sight reverses direction. That reversal is exactly what produces the retrograde part of the loop in the sky.

components.text: Retrograde is a real apparent motion caused by geometry

clips.changeMeaning: After Earth passes Mars, the line of sight resumes eastward progression, completing the causal link between orbital geometry and the observed loop.
clips.narration: After Earth passes Mars, the line of sight resumes its eastward sweep. Retrograde is not an illusion of the eye; it is a real apparent motion produced by changing geometry.

modules.description: Students use their own imagined motion around a floor-marked orbit to generate a retrograde effect while watching Mars against distant stars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Experience retrograde as a consequence of observer motion.
Relate movement on an inner path to Earth's faster orbit.
Observe how a nearer target shifts against a more distant background.
instructions: Look toward Mars and the distant star panel.
Imagine following the blue floor circle as if you were Earth.
Track how your changing viewpoint alters Mars's apparent direction.

components.text: Your motion changes Mars's apparent position against distant stars

clips.changeMeaning: The observer starts on one side of the floor orbit so students can establish the initial Earth-like viewing direction toward Mars and the background stars.
clips.narration: Now imagine your body taking the role of Earth. Mars stays out in front, while you move around a smaller path.

clips.changeMeaning: The observer advances along the inner orbit to show how a changing viewpoint shifts the apparent direction to Mars relative to the distant starfield.
clips.narration: As you move along the inner circle, Mars appears to slide gradually against the faraway constellations.

components.text: Closest approach produces the backward drift

clips.changeMeaning: The observer reaches the overtaking side of the orbit, emphasizing the moment when the apparent motion reverses because of the observer's own motion.
clips.narration: Near closest approach, the apparent motion reverses. By moving past Mars on the inside track, you create the retrograde effect yourself.

components.text: A full circuit reproduces the retrograde pattern

clips.changeMeaning: The observer completes the loop, reinforcing that sustained motion around the inner path reproduces normal drift, reversal, and return.
clips.narration: Completing the circuit recreates the whole pattern: normal drift, reversal, and return. Retrograde is a natural outcome of moving observation points.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
modules.description: Students compare the retrograde loops of multiple outer planets and relate smaller loops to greater distance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare typical retrograde loop sizes for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain why more distant outer planets show smaller angular loops.
Connect loop size to parallax-like viewing geometry.
instructions: Compare each outer planet in turn.
Notice that Earth stays the same while the planet's distance changes.
Focus on how larger distance reduces the angular sweep.

components.text: Mars ~15°   |   Jupiter ~10°   |   Saturn ~7°

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is highlighted first to establish the largest of the three retrograde loops as the reference case for comparison.
clips.narration: Mars usually shows the most dramatic retrograde loop of these three outer planets, roughly fifteen degrees across.

components.text: Jupiter is farther away, so the loop is smaller: about 10°

clips.changeMeaning: Jupiter replaces Mars so students can compare a more distant outer planet whose loop is still visible but less dramatic in angular extent.
clips.narration: Jupiter is farther away, so Earth's motion shifts its apparent direction by a smaller angle. Its loop is typically around ten degrees.

components.text: Saturn is farther still, with a loop of about 7°

clips.changeMeaning: Saturn is shown as the most distant example, reinforcing the trend toward smaller retrograde loops with increasing distance.
clips.narration: Saturn is even farther away, so the same motion of Earth subtends an even smaller angle. Its retrograde loop is typically only about seven degrees across.

components.text: Greater distance means smaller apparent shift, like parallax

clips.changeMeaning: All three planets are displayed together to summarize the distance trend and connect loop size to familiar parallax-style geometry.
clips.narration: The pattern is the same for all three planets. More distant objects shift less against the background when the observer moves, just as in parallax, so their retrograde loops are smaller.

modules.description: Students explore orbital geometry by moving Mars to positions that produce retrograde motion from Earth.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict when retrograde occurs from relative Earth-Mars geometry.
Identify opposition as the key configuration for an outer planet's retrograde episode.
Generalize the prediction rule across different Earth positions.
instructions: Imagine dragging Mars around its orbit while Earth remains fixed.
Use the inset view to judge whether Mars would appear retrograde from Earth.
Look for positions near opposition, where Earth is poised to overtake Mars.

components.text: Place Mars near opposition to produce retrograde

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is initially placed away from opposition so students begin from a non-retrograde configuration and reason toward the correct geometry.
clips.narration: Here Earth is fixed, and Mars can be moved around its orbit. Your goal is to find where Mars must be for retrograde motion to be observed from Earth.

components.text: Hint: retrograde occurs near opposition, when Earth is catching up

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is shifted closer to the opposition side and a hint is added, helping students connect retrograde with overtaking geometry rather than a fixed absolute direction.
clips.narration: The key is opposition: the configuration in which Earth lies between the Sun and Mars and is poised to overtake it from the inside track.

components.text: Correct region: Mars near opposition produces retrograde

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is placed into the correct arc near opposition to confirm the target geometry and demonstrate what a successful prediction looks like.
clips.narration: When Mars is placed in this opposition region, the inset sky view would show retrograde behavior. The relative geometry is what matters.

components.text: With Earth elsewhere on its orbit, look for the same relative alignment

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is moved to a different orbital position and Mars is repositioned correspondingly, reinforcing that retrograde depends on relative alignment rather than absolute scene direction.
clips.narration: Now Earth is somewhere else on its orbit. The rule stays the same: look for the same relative alignment, with Earth on the inside track catching up near opposition.

modules.description: Students review the main ideas from the lab as each concept area is highlighted in turn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the observed retrograde pattern.
Differentiate geocentric and heliocentric explanations.
State the geometric prediction rule and the distance rule for loop size.
instructions: Review the summary points as they highlight one by one.
Use this recap to connect the previous scenes into one explanation.
Be prepared to explain retrograde from both sky-view and orbital perspectives.

components.text:
1. Observed loop
2. Geocentric epicycles
3. Heliocentric resolution
4. Linking geometry to appearance
5. Outer-planet comparison and prediction
Review begins
Observed phenomenon: eastward drift, westward loop, eastward return

clips.changeMeaning: The first summary highlight revisits the observed sky pattern so students begin the recap from the original evidence that required explanation.
clips.narration: First, remember the observed phenomenon itself: Mars usually drifts eastward, reverses into a westward loop, and then returns to eastward motion.

components.text: Geocentric model fits loops with epicycles; heliocentric model explains them more simply

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight shifts from observation to model comparison, emphasizing explanatory simplicity as a scientific reason for preferring heliocentrism.
clips.narration: Second, the geocentric model can fit the loop using epicycles, but the heliocentric model explains the same observation with a simpler underlying geometry.

components.text: Retrograde occurs when faster Earth overtakes a slower outer planet near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: The summary now foregrounds the predictive geometric rule so students can apply the concept beyond the single Mars example.
clips.narration: Third, retrograde occurs when Earth, moving faster on its inner orbit, overtakes a slower outer planet near opposition.

components.text: More distant planets show smaller loops because Earth's motion shifts them by a smaller angle

clips.changeMeaning: The final highlight consolidates the cross-planet comparison and ends the lab with a transferable distance-based explanation of loop size.
clips.narration: Finally, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn all show retrograde, but more distant planets produce smaller loops because the same motion of Earth changes their apparent direction by a smaller angle.
